title: Practice a safe coordination sequence before adding speed
goal: Distinguish power, speed, reaction and coordination, then improve control of one low-risk movement sequence before considering any faster or more forceful version.
scope_note: A tabletop coordination drill does not demonstrate athletic power, running agility or fall-response ability. High-force, ballistic and sport-specific training require suitable conditioning and qualified instruction.
burden: Ten minutes of setup and two five-minute practice sessions with rest.
setup: Place three large colored or labeled cards on a table within comfortable reach. Default sequence: touch left, center, right, then center, using a finger or accessible pointer. Keep the arm supported as needed. The initial target is four correct contacts at a comfortable pace; no timer, impact, competition or forced speed is required.

actions.title: Separate the skill components and fix the safe sequence
actions.instructions: Explain the distinctions using the default: coordination is the correct ordered movement, reaction is responding to an unexpected cue, speed is how quickly the sequence occurs, and power concerns rapid force rather than this light touch. Select the reachable card spacing and support. Fix accuracy criteria—correct order, intended target, controlled movement and no symptom-provoking reach—before starting.
checks: Coordination reaction speed and power are distinguished
Card spacing support and movement are safe for current ability
Four accuracy and control criteria are fixed in advance
The drill is not represented as a power or athletic test

actions.title: Practice accuracy and correct one specific error
actions.instructions: Attempt the sequence three times at a comfortable pace with a short rest between attempts. Record which contact was missed or out of order, then change one cue such as numbering the cards or speaking the sequence. Retry at the same pace. Stop with pain, fatigue or loss of control; do not make the drill harder simply because an error occurred.
checks: Three bounded attempts or an appropriate stop are recorded
Errors are located in a specific contact or transition
One cue correction is tested at the same pace
Accuracy and symptom limits take priority over speed

actions.title: Test a small transfer without claiming broad agility
actions.instructions: On another suitable day, try the sequence with labels in a new order or a willing partner giving one unhurried cue. Change only one feature and keep the same comfortable reach. Compare accuracy, control and cue dependence. Decide whether more basic practice, a different adaptation or qualified sport instruction is the next step; faster is optional and is not required for completion.
checks: A second session changes only one sequence or cue feature
Accuracy control and cue dependence are compared
The adaptation remains safe and comfortable
Athletic power speed and agility remain explicitly untested

adaptation: Use eye gaze, a switch, larger targets, verbal selection or an existing therapist-approved movement. Preserve the intended sequencing or reaction skill while labeling the different motor demands. No catching a falling person, fast direction changes, jumping or heavy lifting is part of the exercise.
review: Did the correction improve the intended movement sequence, and which other physical capacities would need separate training?

examples.supportive: Numbered cards reduced order errors and the new layout was completed with controlled contacts at the same pace.
examples.mixed: Accuracy improved with spoken cues but did not transfer when the cue changed, so cue dependence remained visible.
examples.contradictory: The person accelerated through pain or described a tabletop sequence as proof of athletic power.
examples.inconclusive: A fast time was reported without fixed accuracy criteria or an observed sequence.
